strengths: The paper addresses a practical problem: improving vision–language retrieval through joint reranking while reducing online computation and cached-feature storage. The architecture is straightforward and clearly motivated.
Table 1 reports substantial Recall@1 improvements across four backbone families. With SigLIP2-Large, text-to-image Recall@1 improves from 82.3 to 87.8 on Flickr30k.

The reported compression tradeoff is promising: reducing 576 visual tokens to 64 lowers storage from 442 kB to 49 kB while reducing Flickr text-to-image Recall@1 from 87.8 to 86.9. Table 2 appropriately evaluates prior joint encoders with cached vision features as well.

Ablations examine token count, reranking depth, auxiliary objectives, and distillation. The distillation experiment demonstrates a substantial benefit for the compressed model, improving Recall@1 from 83.8 to 86.9.
weaknesses: The large-scale deployment claim is insufficiently validated. Evaluation uses standard Flickr30k and COCO benchmarks, with no large distractor corpus or end-to-end retrieval experiment. GPU batch timings exclude the practical costs of fetching cached tokens, transferring them to the GPU, and first-stage retrieval. Random disk access, concurrent queries, and tail latency could materially change the claimed throughput.

Table 1 contains an evaluation inconsistency: reranking exactly the top 10 candidates cannot change Recall@10 when the candidate set is unchanged. Nevertheless, CLIP-L/14 at resolution 336 improves image-to-text Recall@10 from 99.0 to 99.9, and several other rows also change. These discrepancies require correction or an explanation of a different evaluation protocol.

Efficiency accounting is not sufficiently controlled or documented. The abstract claims 50,000 pairs/second, whereas Table 2 reports 64 pairs in 1.91 ms, approximately 33,500 pairs/second. Furthermore, baseline storage figures appear consistent with FP32 features, while EDJE storage corresponds to FP16. Storage precision, inference precision, timing methodology, and implementation optimizations must be standardized or explicitly justified.

Novelty is limited relative to the framing. Offline visual-feature caching, learned-query attention pooling, compact pretrained language encoders, and teacher–student distillation are established components. The paper does not convincingly distinguish its compression mechanism from existing query-based resamplers, or compare against simple pooling, token selection, or comparable compressed cached-feature baselines.

The comparisons do not isolate architectural improvements from stronger pretrained representations. EDJE uses SigLIP2 while the main joint-encoder baselines use different visual representations and training histories. Reporting only subsequent training-set sizes obscures this difference. Matched-backbone comparisons and fine-tuned dual-encoder controls would strengthen attribution. The claim of matching prior art also needs qualification: the 64-token model trails BLIP-2 on COCO by 1.7 points for text-to-image and 2.6 points for image-to-text Recall@1.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the hyperparameter appendix. Training duration, training batch size, objective weights, and the precise two-phase training schedule are missing. Section 4 describes text-embedding recovery, but Appendix B labels the corresponding objective image–text contrastive learning. The training mixture is described as 14M pairs in the text and 12M in Table 2. These ambiguities impede reproduction and interpretation of the ablations.

The evaluation does not establish generalization beyond conventional caption retrieval or report uncertainty across runs. Fine-grained compositional retrieval and domain-shift tests would be particularly relevant to claims about richer cross-modal discrimination. Overall, the promising engineering results do not yet overcome the evaluation inconsistencies and missing evidence for the central scalability claim.

strengths: Addresses a practical retrieval problem with a coherent architecture: cached visual features, learned token compression, and a compact MiniLM joint encoder.
Table 1 reports consistent Recall@1 improvements across four backbone families. SigLIP2-L text-to-image retrieval improves from 82.3 to 87.8 on Flickr30k.
The reported compression tradeoff is promising: reducing 576 tokens to 64 lowers storage from 442 kB to 49 kB while reducing Flickr text-to-image Recall@1 from 87.8 to 86.9.
Ablations examine token count, candidate-pool size, auxiliary objectives, and distillation; Table 5 shows a substantial benefit from distillation.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and insufficiently isolated. Feature caching, compact pretrained language encoders, and learned-query attention pooling are established ingredients. The paper lacks comparisons against simpler pooling or token-selection methods and comparable query-based adapters under matched training and storage budgets.

Table 1 conflicts with the stated top-10 reranking protocol. Reordering exactly ten candidates must preserve Recall@10, yet several entries change, including CLIP-L/14 at resolution 336, whose image-to-text Recall@10 increases from 99.0 to 99.9. This requires clarification or correction before the evaluation can be trusted.

The central large-scale deployment claim is not demonstrated. Experiments use Flickr30k and COCO, and timings measure joint encoding rather than a complete retrieval pipeline. There are no large-corpus experiments, disk-fetch measurements, end-to-end query latencies, or concurrent-serving results to establish that cached features deliver the claimed practical throughput.

Efficiency comparisons are insufficiently controlled. Although Table 2 appropriately excludes vision encoding for all methods, numerical precision and implementation details are unspecified. Its baseline storage figures appear consistent with FP32 features, whereas EDJE's figures imply FP16, potentially exaggerating storage savings. Furthermore, 64 pairs in 1.91 ms implies approximately 33,500 pairs/second, not the abstract's 50,000; the latter lacks a documented measurement configuration.

Comparisons confound architecture with backbone quality and prior training. EDJE uses SigLIP2 while the principal joint-encoder baselines use different visual representations. The training-data column does not account for inherited backbone pretraining, and the reported EDJE data count is inconsistent between Section 5.1 (14M pairs) and Table 2 (12M). Matched-backbone comparisons are needed to attribute the gains.

Reproducibility is incomplete: training batch size, training duration, loss weights, and detailed timing procedures are missing. Appendix B describes the third objective as image-text contrastive learning, whereas Section 4 defines text-only embedding recovery. Code and checkpoints are promised rather than supplied.
The evaluation supports a useful engineering proof of concept, but does not yet establish a sufficiently distinctive and rigorously validated contribution for acceptance at a top-tier conference.

strengths: EDJE addresses a practically important problem with a clear architecture: cached visual features, learned token compression, and a compact joint encoder.
Table 1 demonstrates consistent Recall@1 improvements across four backbone families. With SigLIP2-L, Flickr30k text-to-image Recall@1 improves from 82.3 to 87.8.

The reported compression tradeoff is promising: reducing cached tokens from 576 to 64 lowers storage from 442 kB to 49 kB while reducing Flickr30k text-to-image Recall@1 by only 0.9 points. Training-objective and distillation ablations provide useful supporting evidence.
Table 2 explicitly evaluates competing joint encoders with cached visual features, appropriately avoiding charging only the baselines for online vision encoding.
weaknesses: The central large-scale deployment claim is insufficiently validated. Evaluation uses small, standard caption-retrieval benchmarks, without a large distractor corpus or end-to-end measurements including disk reads, feature transfer, candidate retrieval, and query latency. GPU joint-encoding time alone does not establish practical throughput over disk-backed collections.

Efficiency reporting needs reconciliation. Table 2's 64 pairs in 1.91 ms implies approximately 33,500 pairs/second, rather than the abstract's 50,000. Numerical precision, timing methodology, and implementation optimizations are unspecified. Storage figures also appear consistent with FP32 baseline features but FP16 EDJE features, making the reported storage comparison potentially misleading.

The retrieval results contain a concrete protocol inconsistency. Reranking a fixed top-10 candidate set must preserve Recall@10, yet Table 1 changes it in several cases, including CLIP-L/14 at resolution 336, whose image-to-text Recall@10 increases from 99.0 to 99.9. This requires correction or an explanation of a different evaluation procedure.

Novelty is primarily an integration of established components: offline feature caching, learned-query attention pooling, compact language encoders, and distillation. Comparisons against simple pooling or token selection, alternative resamplers, and compact cross-attention models with matched backbones are missing. These controls are necessary to establish the particular architecture's contribution.

Accuracy comparisons confound architecture with pretrained visual representations and training histories. Using SigLIP2 does not match older encoders merely because input resolution matches, and the training-data column excludes upstream backbone pretraining. The compressed model also trails BLIP-2 on COCO by 1.7 points in text-to-image and 2.6 points in image-to-text Recall@1, qualifying the claim of matching prior art.

Reproducibility is incomplete: training batch size, training duration, loss weights, and the detailed phase schedule are missing. Section 4 describes cosine text-embedding recovery, whereas Appendix B labels the corresponding objective image-text contrastive learning. The stated 14M training pairs also need reconciliation with Table 2's 12M designation. Code and checkpoints are promised rather than supplied.

strengths: EDJE addresses a practical retrieval problem with a coherent architecture combining cached visual features, learned token compression, and a compact joint encoder.

Retrieval gains span several backbone families. With SigLIP2-L, the local variant improves Flickr30k text-to-image R@1 from 82.3 to 87.8; compression to 64 tokens retains 86.9 while reducing storage to approximately 49 kB per image.

The appendices provide useful experiments on compression alternatives, distillation, negative mining, quantization, language-encoder choice, and storage I/O. Learned compression consistently outperforms the evaluated subsampling, clustering, and pruning alternatives.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: cached visual features, learned-query compression, compact multimodal transformers, and distillation are established ingredients. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish its contribution from Q-Former-style compression and earlier cached-feature rerankers. Its dismissal of region-feature joint encoders as essentially embedding models is not technically justified.

The central efficiency comparison is insufficiently controlled. Table 2's baseline storage figures are consistent with FP32 features, whereas EDJE uses two-byte features, apparently inflating the storage advantage. Timing precision, attention implementations, synchronization, and warm-up procedures are unspecified. Moreover, 64 pairs in 1.91 ms corresponds to approximately 33,500 pairs/second, leaving the headline 50,000-pairs/second claim unexplained.

The reported retrieval results conflict with the stated top-10 reranking protocol. Reranking a fixed set of ten candidates cannot change Recall@10, yet Table 1 reports changes, including CLIP-L/14@336 image-to-text R@10 increasing from 99.0 to 99.9. This requires correction or an explicit explanation of differing candidate-generation procedures.

The large-scale deployment claim remains only partially supported. Appendix F evaluates larger candidate pools but compares only against LightningDOT, omitting the underlying SigLIP2 retriever and competitive cached joint encoders. Appendix C measures isolated I/O rather than complete retrieval throughput or latency, and does not specify controls for operating-system caching.

Accuracy comparisons confound architecture with visual-backbone quality and inherited pretraining. EDJE uses SigLIP2, while the principal joint-encoder baselines use older backbones. Reporting only EDJE's additional training data also understates its dependence on pretrained representations. Matched-backbone comparisons would better establish the contribution.

Training is not sufficiently reproducible: training batch size, duration, loss weights, and phase-specific objectives are missing. Appendix B calls the third objective image-text contrastive learning, whereas Section 4 describes text-embedding recovery; the reported training-data total also varies between 12M and 14M. These ambiguities matter because the auxiliary objectives and distillation account for substantial gains.

strengths: EDJE addresses a practical retrieval problem with a coherent architecture: cached visual features, learned token compression, and a compact joint encoder separate offline image processing from online reranking.

The reported accuracy–storage trade-off is promising. With 64 tokens, EDJE achieves 86.9/96.4 Flickr30k text-to-image/image-to-text R@1, versus 87.8/96.5 for its uncompressed variant, while reducing storage from 442 to 49 kB per image.

Experiments demonstrate reranking gains across four visual-backbone families. The appendices provide useful comparisons against alternative compression methods and ablations of training objectives, distillation, negative mining, quantization, and language-encoder choice.

The evaluation includes cached-feature comparisons with existing joint encoders, full-dataset retrieval experiments, and preliminary SSD measurements, showing awareness of practical deployment considerations.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited and insufficiently distinguished from prior work. Offline visual features, joint multimodal transformers, learned-query attention pooling, and teacher–student distillation are established ideas. The discussion dismisses region-feature joint encoders as closer to embedding models without adequate justification: compressing regions into vectors does not prevent joint cross-modal interaction. Comparisons with closely related learned-query compressors are needed to establish what the proposed adapter contributes beyond this combination.

The headline efficiency claims are not adequately substantiated. Table 2 reports 1.91 ms for 64 pairs, approximately 33,500 pairs/second, rather than the abstract's 50,000; no corresponding benchmark configuration explains the difference. Precision, software optimizations, synchronization, and timing methodology are insufficiently documented. Baseline storage figures also appear to assume FP32 features, whereas EDJE uses FP16/BF16: 576×768×4 bytes reproduces the reported 1,769 kB for the base baselines. Without consistent precision and implementation settings, the advertised efficiency ratios are difficult to assess.

Architecture and backbone improvements are confounded. EDJE uses modern SigLIP2 features while its main joint-encoder competitors use older visual representations and different training histories. Reporting only joint-model training data also omits the substantial inherited pretraining of the frozen backbone. Matched-backbone comparisons and an appropriately trained embedding-only baseline would better isolate EDJE's architectural contribution.

The large-scale deployment claim exceeds the evidence. Accuracy experiments remain confined to Flickr30k and COCO; the full-dataset extension compares only against LightningDOT, without a modern retriever-only reference. Appendix C measures token reads separately on a 100k-image index, without documenting cold-cache behavior or measuring integrated retrieval, transfer, and reranking latency. This does not establish end-to-end throughput or latency at the million-to-billion-image scale motivating the paper.

Reproducibility and reporting contain consequential gaps. Appendix A omits training duration, training batch size, and loss weights. Section 4 describes text-embedding recovery, but Appendix B labels the corresponding ablation as image–text contrastive learning. Training-data totals differ between Section 5.1 and Table 2. Moreover, Table 1 changes CLIP-L/14@336 image-to-text R@10 from 99.0 to 99.9 despite the stated top-10-only reranking protocol, which should preserve candidate-set R@10. These discrepancies require resolution.

The interpretability conclusions are stronger than their evidence. Nearest-vocabulary-token assignments do not establish that features mapping to special tokens lack semantic information. The alignment analysis lacks mismatched-caption controls, and Figure 9's caption describes a downward shift while the reported means show an upward shift. These analyses should be presented as exploratory rather than evidence of semantic preservation.

strengths: EDJE addresses a practical problem with a coherent design: cached, compressed visual tokens combined with a compact joint encoder substantially reduce online computation and storage.

Retrieval improvements are consistent across several visual backbones. On Flickr30k, local EDJE improves SigLIP2-L text-to-image R@1 from 82.3 to 87.8; compression to 64 tokens retains 86.9 while reducing storage from 442 kB to 49 kB per image.

The supplementary experiments provide useful evidence beyond the main results, including compression baselines, training-objective and distillation ablations, quantization, negative-mining variations, and language-encoder comparisons. The learned adapter outperforms the tested compression alternatives under a shared training protocol.

The paper considers deployment concerns through expanded candidate pools and SSD access measurements. Comparing prior joint encoders with cached visual features is also an appropriate experimental choice.
weaknesses: The efficiency comparison needs stronger controls and clearer reporting. Table 2's 1.91 ms for 64 pairs implies approximately 33,500 pairs/second, rather than the abstract's 50,000. Baseline storage figures appear consistent with FP32 visual tokens, whereas EDJE uses BF16/FP16, potentially inflating relative storage savings. Matched precision, attention implementations, timing methodology, and clearly separated compute and end-to-end throughput are necessary to substantiate the headline claims.

The reported retrieval results conflict with the stated top-10 reranking protocol. Reordering exactly ten candidates must preserve Recall@10, yet Table 1 reports changes, including CLIP-L/14 at resolution 336 improving image-to-text R@10 from 99.0 to 99.9. This requires correction or an explanation of an additional retrieval step.

The conceptual novelty is limited: offline feature caching, compact multimodal transformers, learned-query compression, and distillation are established ingredients. The paper should distinguish its contribution more precisely from cached region-feature joint encoders and Q-Former-style compression. Describing region-based joint rerankers as effectively embedding models is not convincing merely because each region has one vector.

The evidence for large-scale retrieval remains limited. Appendix F compares against LightningDOT without reporting the underlying SigLIP2 retriever or contemporary joint-encoder baselines, so the incremental benefit of EDJE in the expanded pools is unclear. The isolated SSD benchmark is useful but does not establish complete retrieval-service performance or billion-image scalability.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite Appendix A. Training duration, training batch size, loss weights, and the precise pretraining/fine-tuning schedule are missing. Section 4 specifies text-embedding recovery, whereas Appendix B describes the corresponding objective as image-text contrastive learning; the manuscript also alternates between 12M and 14M training pairs.

Comparisons do not fully isolate the contribution of the architecture from the stronger pretrained SigLIP2 backbone, and training-data counts omit inherited backbone pretraining. EDJE offers an attractive efficiency tradeoff, but its compressed variant remains below BLIP-2 on COCO R@1, particularly image-to-text retrieval (80.9 versus 83.5). Overall, the practical promise is substantial, but unresolved evaluation and reporting issues place the submission slightly below the acceptance threshold.
